edits.english: The mishna teaches similar cases, including the case of one who left a gentile in his shop, and the case of one who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship. The Gemara explains: And it is necessary for the mishna to cite all these cases, even though they appear similar, as, had the mishna taught only the case of the gentile transporting a Jew’s barrels, one might assume that the reason there is no concern that the gentile used the wine in that case is because the gentile thinks that perhaps the owner will come and see him. But in a wagon or on a ship, one might say that the gentile can take his ship far off and do what he desires in such a way that the owner cannot see him.
As, had it taught a gentile - A gentile who was transporting barrels of wine:
And do what he desires - And even if the owner did not inform the gentile that he was going far off, the wine would be forbidden:

We learned in the Mishna several similar rulings: One who leaves a gentile in his shop, etc. One who places his wine in a wagon or on a ship, etc. And they comment: And it is necessary [and this Mishna needed] to state all the cases described in it, even though they seemingly are all similar in content, as, had [if it had taught] only the case of a gentile transporting barrels, we would say: There is no concern there, because [the gentile] thinks: Perhaps the owner will come and see him. But in a wagon or on a ship—[say] that he can take his ship far off and do what he desires in a way that the Israelite cannot see him.

And had the mishna taught only the case where the Jew placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship, one might assume that the concern there is because the gentile thinks: Perhaps the Israelite will come on a different road or stand on the bank of the river and see him. But in the case of a gentile in his shop, one might say that the gentile can hold the door closed and do whatever he desires with no concern of being seen. Therefore, the mishna teaches us that in all of these cases the same ruling applies, and there is no concern unless the Jew informed the gentile that he is going a great distance away.

And had [if it had taught] **in a wagon or on a ship,** we would say: There, the gentile is concerned **because he thinks: Perhaps the Israelite will come on a different road or stand on the bank of the river and see him.** But in the case of **a gentile in his shop,** [say] that **he can hold,** close, **the door and do whatever he desires** and is not concerned that he might be seen. **It teaches us** that in all cases the ruling is the same, and there is no concern unless the owner informed the gentile that he is going far off.
